Thought: Three reviewers, all Overall 5 / Reject / Confidence 4, and they agree closely. I checked their main factual claims against the paper text, and all hold: only the full-text arm of the hidden-full-text experiment was repaired (Fig. 2 caption; Sec. 4.1); the planted-error test has no unaltered controls (Sec. 4.4); there is no development split (Limitation vi); one model family does every step and no human validated anything (abstract; Limitation i); the Table 1 'Supp.' column is captioned 'after repair', but the memory-only control is 'audited but not repaired' (Sec. 3.2); the header reads ICLR 2025. Agreed strengths: a clean design where only the strategy varies; fixed fact lists split once; careful statistics (completion treated as an outcome, ITT sensitivity, replicate-noise floor, sign tests, Holm); a paired within-paper access experiment; a matched ablation; candid limitations. Agreed weaknesses, in order of weight: (1) the whole measurement chain is unvalidated same-family model judgement, at the 1-2 point resolution the conclusions use; (2) one model, so 'strategies are close' may be model-specific; (3) the headline access effect is close to expected given how the reference is built, and its arms are asymmetric; (4) 'strategies are close' is shown in a regime (81% abstract/title-only, 2-12 references, no inputs beyond one prompt) that compresses differences, and the regime where they differ is small and observational; (5) no development set; (6) the audit test has no specificity measure. R1 adds a point I find important and the paper does not resolve: pooled direct-reading coverage of abstract-only papers is 40.1%, yet only 2% of the missed abstract-only facts are stated in the abstract, and abstract-only coverage varies with creation era (Sec. 4.5). So part of what counts as 'read from the abstract' may be recall cued by the abstract, which the memory-only control (about 15%) does not bound. This bears on the 77.4 vs 31.2 contrast and on the strategy comparison. Novelty and venue fit for ICLR are modest; this is a benchmark/empirical study. Presentation is precise but very dense. Decision: Reject. The work is careful and honest, but the primary endpoint is unvalidated and the main null rests on one model. A human agreement study on a sample, a second model on a subset, a symmetric access comparison and a cued-recall analysis would make this a strong benchmark paper.
Summary: The paper presents a controlled benchmark for writing curated genetics knowledge-base entries. Each of 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references each, stratified by creation era) is rewritten by one model (Claude Opus 5.5) from its header and exactly the papers its curators cited, with the causal gene withheld and only open-access text available (19% of papers in full text, no supplements). Generation, guards, claim-level audit with one repair round, and scoring are shared, so the generation strategy is the only variable. Strategies cover three paradigms: read and write (direct reading, agentic curator); extract, then write (evidence graph, case table); and memory first (recall, then verify). There is also a memory-only control and three add-ons (second-hand evidence from citing papers, case reconciliation, a learned curation guide). The primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed', is coverage of fixed fact lists split once, without sight of any draft, from OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs deposited in ClinVar (6,652 facts). Secondary measures are HPO synopsis terms, variants, causal gene and inheritance. Main results: on 93 jointly completed entries the reading strategies score 47.2-49.1%, and only the case table (-1.9) exceeds the 1.0-point replicate-noise half-width; memory-based strategies score about 15%. Hiding the full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 77.4% to 31.2% (46 entries; +43.9 points paired). Strategy differences appear larger where more full text is readable (21-25 entries, observational). A matched ablation attributes much of the extract-then-write deficit to extraction effort. The audit flags all 60 planted single-fact substitutions but checks fidelity to the source, not correctness. Second-hand evidence gives +1.8 points at a cost in unsupported claims. The learned guide and reconciliation are nulls. Memory-only performance by creation era serves as a contamination check.
Strengths: Clean experimental control: model, sources, guards, audit and scoring are held fixed, so the generation strategy is the only manipulated variable. This addresses a real comparability gap in prior work (FlyAOC, WikiCrow, GEN-KnowRD), which varies several factors at once or scores against something other than per-paper curator text (all reviewers).

Careful evaluation design: fact lists are split once without sight of any draft and reused for every strategy, avoiding draft-adaptive denominators. The paper reports that earlier per-draft scoring inflated levels (all reviewers).

Unusually careful statistics for LLM-pipeline comparisons. Completion, including safety-filter stops, is treated as an outcome, and comparisons use jointly completed entries with a missing-as-zero sensitivity analysis. There is a measured replicate-noise floor (3 replicates on 30 entries) and judge-variation estimates, plus paired bootstrap intervals, sign counts and Holm correction. A previously biased analysis (the -2.1 evidence-graph gap) is documented and corrected (all reviewers).

The within-paper hidden-full-text experiment (same papers, same 2,120 facts, paired over 46 entries) and the missed-fact attribution give direct evidence that, in this setting, input access rather than strategy bounds agreement with curators (all reviewers).
The matched ablation separates extraction effort from the intermediate representation and tempers an otherwise over-reaching negative claim about extract-then-write (all reviewers).

Candid scoping and limitations. The paper distinguishes 'judged supported' from correct, shows concretely that the audit checks fidelity rather than truth (second-hand evidence analysis), reports that the planted-error test measures sensitivity only, and states that no human validated any judgement (all reviewers).
A contamination check via creation-era bands plus a set of entries created June-November 2026 (all reviewers).
Built from public resources, with per-entry release of drafts, verdicts and scores and transparent cost accounting (all reviewers).
Weaknesses: No human validation anywhere in the measurement chain. The same model family that writes the drafts also splits curator paragraphs into facts, judges fact presence (the primary endpoint), audits claims, attributes missed facts and adjudicates contradictions. Self-preference bias (cited but not measured) and systematic judge error could shift absolute levels and interact with strategy style, and the conclusions rely on 1-2 point differences. A curator or trained-annotator agreement study on a sample (e.g. 200-500 fact judgements and a sample of audit verdicts) is needed before the primary endpoint can be trusted at that resolution (all reviewers; main soundness gap).

Single model, single family. The central claim that 'the reading strategies are close' is established only for one frontier long-context model. It may not hold for weaker or shorter-context models, where intermediate representations and agentic reading are usually motivated. No second writer or judge was tested even on a subset such as the 30 replicate entries or the 38-entry ablation (all reviewers).

The headline access result is close to expected by construction. The reference was written by curators from full papers (often with supplements), so drafts from abstracts necessarily convey fewer of those facts (cf. Cohen et al., 2010). The quantification is useful but not surprising, and the framing should say so. The comparison is also asymmetric: only the full-text arm went through the repair round, so a pre-repair full-text score or repaired abstract arms are needed (all reviewers).

The 'strategies are close' conclusion comes from a regime that compresses differences: 81% of papers are abstract- or title-only, entries have 2-12 references, and no input exceeds one prompt. The regime where strategies differ (half or more full text, 21 entries; full-text papers in the 38-entry ablation) is small and observational, confounded with era and journal. The main comparison therefore does not test the setting in which the compared designs are expected to differ, and the headline should be framed accordingly (R1, R2, R3).

Cued recall is not separated from reading. Pooled direct-reading coverage on abstract-only papers is 40.1%, yet only 2% of the missed abstract-only facts are stated in the abstract, and abstract-only coverage varies with creation era. A share of facts 'conveyed' from abstracts may therefore come from model memory cued by the abstract, which the memory-only control (about 15%) does not bound. The paper should report what fraction of conveyed abstract-only facts is actually stated in the available text. This affects both the 77.4 vs 31.2 contrast and the strategy comparison (R1; supported by the paper's own Sec. 4.5 caveat).

No separate development set: strategies were designed and tuned on the evaluation entries. Given the small effects being interpreted, this could favour whichever strategy received the most iteration (likely the direct-reading baseline). Evaluating all strategies on a fresh held-out sample (e.g. the 2026 entries) would address it (all reviewers).

The audit's planted-error test (60/60 flagged) has no unaltered controls, so its false-flag rate is unknown. Only blunt single-value substitutions were tested, and omissions and misattributed citations were not. The 60/60 result is therefore weak evidence about audit quality as a detector (all reviewers).

Narrow, indirect reference. Only variant-centred OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs in ClinVar are used, plus HPO annotations partly derived from OMIM (476 of 2,311); narrative phenotype sections are not compared. Drafts make about twice as many statements as the reference has facts (24.0 vs 11.9), so the correctness and relevance of extra content is unmeasured beyond the audit (R1, R2, R3).

Limited methodological novelty and modest generalisable lesson for ICLR. The strategies are the authors' own re-implementations of known paradigms, and the add-ons are deliberately minimal (two reflection rounds on 27 entries for the learned guide; recall-then-verify may not add content), so their nulls are largely uninformative. The value is mainly a domain benchmark whose curator text cannot be redistributed (R1, R2, R3).

Presentation is very dense: many sentences carry several numbers with intervals, and the reader must track many entry subsets (100, 97, 96, 93, 49/46, 40/38, 30, 20). Minor errors: the Table 1 'Supp.' column is captioned 'after repair', but the memory-only control is never repaired; the running header reads 'ICLR 2025' while citing 2026 work; the agentic curator's interval (-1.3, +0.0) touches zero with sign counts 31/42/20 leaning negative, yet it is described as within noise; the missing-as-zero sensitivity intervals (e.g. -3.0 to +3.1) are too wide to support 'the same picture' on their own (R1, R2, R3).
Questions: Can you provide human (curator or trained annotator) agreement data for fact-list splitting, present/partly/absent/contradicted judgements and a sample of audit verdicts, reported per category? Does judge error differ by strategy, and would the strategy ordering survive the observed disagreement rate?

Have you run any strategy comparison, even on the 30 replicate entries or the 38-entry ablation, with a second model family as writer and/or as judge on fixed drafts? Does the closeness of the reading strategies hold for a weaker or shorter-context model?
In the hidden-full-text experiment, what is full-text coverage before the repair round, so that all three conditions are compared without repair?

For abstract-only papers, what fraction of the facts the drafts conveyed is actually stated in the abstract? How do you separate reading from cued recall, and how does this affect the 77.4% vs 31.2% contrast?

How were the strategies developed? Which entries were inspected during prompt and pipeline design, and how much iteration did each strategy receive? Can all strategies be evaluated on a fresh held-out set (e.g. the 2026 entries)?
What is the audit's false-flag rate on unaltered paragraphs, and how does it handle omissions and misattributed citations?
For draft content beyond the reference facts, can you estimate what fraction is correct and relevant (e.g. audit plus a human sample)?

Is there a regime (larger reference lists, inputs beyond one prompt, weaker models, papers with supplements) where extract-then-write or agentic reading outperforms direct reading? What does the 30-75-reference tier show? Can the strategy-by-full-text effect be tested within entries using the ablation set?
Are the synopsis results different when restricted to the HPO team's own curation (1,835 annotations) rather than the 476 taken from OMIM?
Why is replicate noise used as a separate threshold rather than incorporated into the intervals (e.g. a hierarchical bootstrap over entries and replicates)?
Given that curator text cannot be redistributed, how will others reproduce the reference fact lists and scores exactly?
Limitations: The authors' limitations section is thorough and candid: single model family, no human validation, narrow indirect reference, open-access text only without supplements, reference list given, no development split, uneven stopped replies, small entries only. These should weigh more heavily in how the main conclusions are framed, especially 'reading strategies are close'.
Not fully addressed: cued recall of facts from abstract-only papers, and judge self-preference interacting differently with different strategies.
The access result should be framed explicitly as partly a consequence of how the reference is constructed (curator text written from full text and supplements).
Small evaluation sets (93 compared entries; 46 in the access experiment; 38 in the ablation; 21 in the high-full-text group); results do not cover inputs larger than one prompt or weaker models.
Safety-filter refusals remove entries unevenly across strategies, and their reasons are not visible.
The generated entries could be mistaken for curated content; the ethics statement appropriately requires labelling them as machine-generated drafts for expert review.
